utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, would you have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. You see the judges are not wearing their robes. As we said, Judge Shahabuddeen, for exceptional circumstances, is in Arusha. Therefore, what I would suggest is that there might be an oral motion brought from the side of the Defence or an oral motion from the Prosecution. In order to simplify the operations, I would like an agreement from the -- I see there's no transcript. My words have not been put into writing. You see, that's very important, as Mr. Dubuisson says. But having said that, let me turn to my colleague. We're going to adjourn this short session. We don't have the transcript. Not only the pilots are striking, we don't have the transcript either. I wanted to be able to save a bit of time here, but that's how things are. All right. We're going to adjourn the hearing, and the registrar will inform us as soon as the transcript is operable again. In the meantime, I would like to point out, even though this is not in the transcript, in order to facilitate our operations and once the transcript is working, I would like the Defence to make a request for exceptional circumstances to hear the witnesses so that those transcripts can be given to Judge Shahabuddeen and the Prosecution would give me their agreement with that. I hope that shortly we will be able to resume our hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 9.56 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I turn to the Defence first. Mr. Hayman, do you agree that we should work in that way as part of Rule 71?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We believe, Mr. President, and good morning Mr. President and Your Honour, that we should use the time this week despite Judge Shahabuddeen's absence. We, of course, know that he will review the record with due care and that that task can be entrusted to him, despite the burdens that it puts on him, and we would so request and join in any request from the Prosecutor to proceed this week by deposition pursuant to the appropriate rule or rules and this Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. Thank you for your contribution to speeding up our work. Now, does the Prosecution agree with the same conditions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the Office of the Prosecutor agrees with the outline of our schedule and the desires as laid out by the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I support all that has been said by my attorney and the position of the Defence and I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. We're not going to render an official decision, but I'll ask that this all be put into the minutes of the registry and filed. All right, we can now continue. Mr. Kehoe, the following witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Judge Riad. The next witness that the Office of the Prosecutor will call is Brigadier Alastair Duncan. From prior testimony, Your Honours may have learned that Brigadier Duncan was then Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, the commanding officer of the Prince of Wales own regiment of Yorkshire. He commanded the British battalion in Vitez from approximately the 11th of May, 1993 to the first week of November 1993. The Prince of Wales own regiment of Yorkshire was the British battalion that took over for the Cheshire Regiment which was the regiment that was in Vitez during the events of 16 April, 1993. Brigadier Duncan, then Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, had numerous contacts with the defendant Blaskic. He will testify concerning the events in Central Bosnia when he got there, specifically the Vitez area, how the events in Ahmici and the Lasva Valley in mid April of 1993 changed the landscape dramatically throughout the Lasva Valley. He will talk about his conversations with not only Blaskic, but his conversations with political leaders from the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, specifically Dario Kordic and Anto Valenta. He will talk about the conclusions that he reached after some of those conversations with Valenta and Kordic, and he will likewise talk about the conclusions he reached after conversations with the accused, when the accused Blaskic gave his very explanation as to what had happened in the attack on Ahmici. Mr. President and Judge Riad, as opposed to being an event-driven testimony, this will be a theme-driven testimony because I think with Brigadier Duncan, the court has the unique opportunity to talk to a man who had contact with the defendant while they were both in the field. From those conversations, the brigadier will testify concerning Blaskic's command, the exercise of that command, how he exercised that command, how he conducted himself as a man with the trappings of a military commander, how he punished soldiers when he deemed it necessary or when he desired to do so. From those indications, we will move to some events, such as the Ahmici event and some other events that will be discussed along the way, and Brigadier Duncan will give you his impressions on how the defendant, a commander who had been trained by the JNA and had been a graduate of the military academy in Belgrade, failed to meet his obligations as a commander. The brigadier will give reasons, based on what he experienced, as to why Blaskic failed to meet his obligations as a commander and, for the most part, we are talking about his failure to meet his obligations as a commander as outlined by international law. He will also talk about Blaskic's failure to act, which is really a subset of his failure to act and failure to meet his obligations as a commander. The brigadier has drawn certain conclusions, some five years down the line, as to what exactly was happening in the Lasva Valley during the period of time when the defendant was under his command. Addressing the indictment and bringing us back to the facts that we just discussed and how they fit into the indictment, much of what we are going to talk about has to do with paragraph 3 and 4 of the indictment which has to do with the description of Blaskic on his authority and responsibility for his troops; number 4, the exercise of his control and the exercise of his command in military matters. Likewise, we will discuss any number of topics but how he exercised his command and what he did and didn't do in his failing to meet his obligations as a commander touches every count in the indictment, because as the indictment addresses, it is a failure to act, a failure to prevent, a failure to punish, as well as an indictment of someone who is directing a particular course of conduct. In any event, Mr. President and Judge Riad, virtually everything that the brigadier will talk about will impact on every count in the indictment. That would be the summary that we would finish with at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How long do you think that this is going to take, that is, your part of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would say two hours, Mr. President, Judge Riad, maybe a little bit longer, but I don't believe that it will take that long. We will not, Mr. President and Judge Riad, conduct an examination which addresses every issue that the brigadier experienced from the raising of the flag to the striking of the colours and we will prevent that type of examination. That's why we attempted to make it a theme-based examination where we would discuss various issues and then allow the brigadier to discuss factual situations and his impressions from those factual situations as he goes through his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am very pleased to hear you say that and I want to say that I agree with what you say, but you really are encouraging me. I can recall to you -- let me take a minute out here. It began on the 23rd of June last year. We are now coming to the celebration of the first anniversary. I think testimony has to be focused around one or two very specific themes and not to have Colonel Duncan to say how the village was burned. We know how it burned. You want to go over his contacts with the accused, the way that he exercised his command, however, in your opinion, he did not. I really ask you to focus on that. We don't necessarily have to have two hours to hear a witness say how he was able to observe what you want to bring out for the judges. All right, you can have Colonel Duncan brought in now. Brigadier, is it? What is his rank, Brigadier General?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He's now a brigadier, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, do you hear me? Could you please tell us your first name and your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Alastair Duncan and I'm a Brigadier General in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing for the time it takes to you read your declaration that the usher is going to give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, you may be seated. General, you have come at the request of the Prosecution as part of the trial of the International Criminal Tribunal against General Blaskic, the accused who is in this courtroom. We have heard the summary of your testimony and we ask you to focus on those points specifically while you testify. We don't have to hear about everything you heard between May and November 1993. We begin on the 23rd of June. Starting from that date, the judges are already familiar with a certain number of things, but in the opinion of your Prosecutor, your testimony is important for a specific number of points, and these have just been stated by the Prosecution who explained it to the judges, and then we will pass after that to the cross-examination. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President ALASTAIR DUNCAN

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier Duncan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, before we go into the actual testimony concerning the events in Central Bosnia, can you just give the judges a little sketch of your background focusing on operational tours and your experience and how it bears on your expertise in infantry matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. I was commissioned to my regiment in 1973 and spent the first 12 months of my life with the regiment in Northern Ireland commanding on operations, a platoon in Belfast. I then moved back to instruct junior soldiers in infantry tactics before moving back to the regiment to be the operations officer and adjutant. After that I moved to the school of infantry for three years where I was responsible for low level tactics and command procedures. After that I went to staff college, both the technical staff college at Shrivenham, England and Camberley which is our main tactics course. After that I went back to the battalion, which was again in Northern Ireland, and commanded again on operations in South Armagh for some 18 months. That followed a period as chief of staff of an infantry brigade which was equipped with armoured vehicles but primarily infantry tactics --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we ask the witness to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I was asked to write the operation orders and to deal with the training of that brigade for fitness in war. Thereafter, I moved back to the staff college as an instructor specialising in infantry vehicles and, again, tactics for operations. After that, I was moved to take over command of my battalion where I commanded it both in Belfast for a six-month operational tour and for seven months in Central Bosnia in 1993. After that, I returned to the staff college where I was responsible for instructing on command and ethics and command control for operational matters. Then I moved to command of an infantry or a mechanised brigade in the north of England where I spent two years, culminating in four months when I returned to Bosnia and took my brigade to multi-national division south-west and commanded there for five months. I have commanded on operations at every level from platoon, company, battalion, brigade and also stood in as a divisional commander, and I have specialised throughout my career in the nature of command, the duties of commanders and specifically infantry work. That is all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Brigadier, can we turn to the period of time that you were just discussing where you were a commanding officer in Bosnia and you were the commanding officer of the Prince of Wales own regiment of Yorkshire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you tell the judges the time frame in which you were the commanding officer in theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went on two reconnaissances in early 1993, each for one week, in January and February, and then after that I deployed and took over in Bosnia from the 11th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. The 11th of March or May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, the 11th of May, 1993 through to November, the middle of November of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During that period of time, you covered an area from approximately where to where? What was the responsibility of the British battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The British battalion was responsible for the supply of aid through to Central Bosnia and up through to North Bosnia to Tuzla. My area of responsibility was from just south of Prozor Lakes right the way through Gornji Vakuf, Vitez, Zenica and on all the way up to Tuzla. I was responsible for that primary aid route into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the period of time you were in theatre, did you have different bases throughout Central Bosnia from which the British battalion operated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had the battalion headquarters in two mixed companies based at Vitez school, a company again mixed based at Gornji Vakuf, and the last company based at Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There was a physical separation between your company and Tuzla and your company in Gornji Vakuf and your headquarters in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very much so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you still responsible for those troops and the actions of those troops in those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Entirely. It was my battalion; it was my command and I was in sole responsibility for all of those actions of my troops under my command which is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was my next question. Is that the normal --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was absolutely standard practise. There is one commander who is directly responsible for all actions of his troops, good or bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the actual events that took place in Central Bosnia during your seven-month tour, and even during your recesses in January and February, and without going through the particular events, could you give the Judges an idea, an overview, as to what transpired during your period of time, a brief overview, if you will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just consult my personal notes? Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These again are notes that have not been shared with the Prosecution and obviously are not subject to the statement disclosure rule, Mr. President and Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please make breaks between questions and answers for the benefit of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, if I may just briefly, because you and I are speaking in English, it's important that between our two comments that we have a slight break. It's something that my colleagues often suffer when it's speaking Serbo-Croatian, but you and I speak English, so if we could just pace ourselves, I think it would be helpful. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, General. You're looking at notes to refresh your memory. You're not reading a report that you prepared in advance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are notes that I made earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: ... for the defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already stated that I took -- did two brief reconnaissances of one week in early 1993. I took over the battalion from Colonel Bob Stewart on the 11th of May and spent a week prior to that, from the 5th to the 11th of May, visiting various commanders and looking at the ground in the area to see what the situation was. I discovered there had been a complete change of mood in the area, since my reconnaissances in that, after the events in Ahmici, there now existed a serious level of suspicion, mistrust, and conflict in Central Bosnia, and that mistrust and conflict was to last for the next 15 months, as far as I'm aware. Certainly, considerably longer after I had finished and left Bosnia in November of that year. That was the situation as I arrived. From then onwards, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is the Muslim forces, made significant advances, inroads into the Croat-held area, and that took place during most of May and June. In July, the conflict spread down to the area of Gornji Vakuf, and that erupted into some very serious fighting. But from then onwards, throughout my time there until I left, the situation became relatively static with a number of Croat pockets, notably around Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak, with the front-line also at Gornji Vakuf, and that was the situation that prevailed throughout my time. The operational command of the HVO was exercised directly from Hotel Vitez, and the command of the 3rd BiH Corps in the area was exercised directly from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During your tour, the command was exercised from the Hotel Vitez; who was the individual that exercised that command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was exercised by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is that individual in the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is sitting in the court in the corner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let the record reflect, Mr. President and Judge Riad, that the witness is identifying the Defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the gentleman seated in the back next to the police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who exercised command of 3rd Corps from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, did you come to learn the level of forces, that then Colonel Blaskic controlled, when you came in May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The British battalion was organised to have a military information cell which collated information gathered in from patrols on the ground and from liaison officers, and from that we had been able to build up a full picture of the command structure of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As the events developed over the course of the summer of 1993 and there were more inroads by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were there some changes in the order of battle prepared and some variations with the Ord. Batt. that you initially drafted concerning the forces controlled by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Sorry, I'll pause. Yes, there were. This had to do with the -- as the Muslim force advances, a number of changes in the Ord. Batt. were made to reflect the fact that positions were no longer occupied by the brigades. These changes were recorded and we made a note of them as they occurred. But I must say, the span of command, that is the distance and areas which were commanded, remained the same throughout. The responsibility was still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, and I have been reminded by my colleague, Mr. Harmon, concerning some of the military vernacular. What is an Ord. Batt.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's an acronym for "Order of Battle" and would be a hierarchical chart in which we could display exactly who a commander was, who his subordinates are, and the command arrangements between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may turn to the first two exhibits, Mr. President, which are two orders of battle that have been prepared, and these were prepared by your subordinates, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could move to the first one without the Xs and then the second one without the Xs? If we could move in that chronology? If we could put the ELMO on, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 378 and 379.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you could, Brigadier Duncan, taking a look at Exhibit 378, the order of battle that was prepared by your subordinates, could you just briefly explain this to the President and Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we need the other one first. I believe that the forward --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm sorry. The one without the Xs first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So if I might briefly explain this? This was prepared by my military information officer, a Captain Simon Harrison, and it shows on the top line in the centre, the Op Zone Central Bosnia, Vitez-Travnik, with a Commander Tihomir Blaskic and a Deputy Commander Franjo Nakic. On the left of that, with a dotted line, because it is not under command or in a command relationship, is the political wing of the HDZ; and on the right, again with a dotted line, is the joint commission that had then been set up in Travnik. Below that, the command splits, a direct command from Tihomir Blaskic's headquarters of the first Ops group on the left, the second Ops group in the centre, and the third Ops group in the right. So below that you can see the brigades, the boxes with a cross on the top, which represented the subordinate forces under command, and those range right the way across, and we have annotated that we knew where they were; for example, the Travnik brigade obviously in Travnik, a brigade in Zenica there, one is Dolac and Guca Gora, Kiseljak, Vares and Kakanj, Sarajevo, Tarcin, Sadovaca and Zepce, and you can therefore see the span and scope of the command which is exercised by Colonel Blaskic's headquarters in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can move, if you will, to the next document, Exhibit 379, with the Xs on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that the number, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is 378, the document that is being shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just clarify for the record? If our numbered sequence is a bit off, 378, the document that is currently on the ELMO with the Xs on it, chronologically comes after the document that we just looked at, 379. So I think that it may be easier, Mr. President, if we can just quickly renumber these documents, and if we can discuss the document without the Xs and call that 378 and the document with the Xs 379, I believe there would be no objection from my colleague across the hall -- across the courtroom. It might be easier for record-keeping purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see crosses everywhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We just try to make it -- if we move chronologically, Mr. President, for record-keeping purposes down the line, it just may be easier to make this a subsequent number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, very well. No problem with that. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, turning to Exhibit 379.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise for the amount of crosses on this piece of paper. It is to do with the military symbology to record size of units. The small crosses are brigade-sized units; the larger crosses, has as just been indicated, are units which have been removed from the order of battle because they no longer exist due to the fighting; and in the notes at the bottom, there is a reference here to the 14th of June when one unit, in this case the one indicated there, had no longer existed, and this is how we kept a record of the span of command throughout the time I was in Bosnia for reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted, Brigadier, during the course of your testimony, that pockets existed, and certainly were firmed up in the summer of 1993, and one of those pockets would be the Vitez-Busovaca pocket and the next one, of course, being the Kiseljak pocket.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the period of time, your orders of battle indicate that Blaskic continued to remain in command of those pockets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very much, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you an article -- and we have an article, a Danish article that has been translated, in part in French and English, and is an interview by a reporter for Danish of the Defendant Blaskic. There are two portions of this interview that we will highlight at this juncture, Mr. President, and we would just like to first talk to the first portion at this time when you get a view of that, Brigadier, we will talk about that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 380.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just discussing the first paragraph in that translation from the article, Brigadier, could you read that first question and answer at the top of the page concerning Kresevo, Kiseljak, and part of the Fojnica municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. It states: "Kresevo, Kiseljak, and part of Fojnica municipality, also controlled by the HVO, are also in Central Bosnia but are not connected with the forces in Vitez and Busovaca. How are they holding up?" And the reply from Blaskic is as follows: "It is certain that the will and determination of the Croatian people in these areas were awakened exceptionally early and resulted in the firm defence of these areas, and I would add Vares here, which is in the structure of our second operative group in Central Bosnia. They are carrying out, in a coordinated and organised manner, all commands connected with the defence of the people and Croatian territories. This physical separation is not an essential or decisive factor because we figured in our planning that the temporary physical separation of these areas could occur. Travnik is the first operative group, Kiseljak the second, Zepce the third, and Sarajevo the fourth. All operative groups under my command and the chain of leadership and command functions absolutely, without interruption."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that consistent with what Blaskic told you, that he commanded these areas and, despite the physical separation, he still had command and control over those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is entirely consistent with what Commander Blaskic told me throughout my time in Bosnia, when I questioned him on a number of occasions, to confirm that he was in command, and he always stated: Yes, he was the commander of the Op zone in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President and Judge Riad, there is another paragraph that we will discuss in that newspaper article at a later date, and we will have the whole article translated in full in both French and English. We just haven't had the opportunity to complete it at this juncture. And with this particular witness, we just wanted to focus on these two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving on, Brigadier, and let us go back from the Ord. Batts. and back to your period of time in Bosnia commanding the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire, and I ask you from the beginning of May through the period of time, with conversations with Blaskic and with political leaders, did you reach concern conclusions as to what the plan of the HVO was in Central Bosnia, and if so, could you tell the Judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I recall that on the 12th of May, I spoke at length with a man called Anto Valenta in his office in Hotel Vitez, which was within the Ops zone Central Bosnia headquarters in Vitez. He presented a book to me, the name of which escapes me -- it is a small blue book -- it was written by Anto Valenta, and it describes how he saw a process of movement of individuals from the various ethnic origins in Bosnia was essential for long-term stability in that country. That movement of individuals was either to be voluntary or coerced or forced, and, in fact, the book on one page refers to the use of the Yugoslav National Army, if necessary, to achieve this aim. I concluded from that that the movement of the population was therefore no longer just a civil matter but something that might need the use of force since the Yugoslav -- he was proposing that the Yugoslav National Army would have to be required to do that. My reply -- I was somewhat surprised because this was very clearly a rather extreme ethnically-based policy to reorganise the country by force, and I told Anto Valenta that I found this concept distasteful and running contrary to all the norms that I knew of behaviour in a civilised country, and I stated that the State must not interfere with the freedoms of individuals in such a drastic and, frankly, unacceptable manner. But I quickly realised that this was the policy of a man who was representing the HDZ party, and I came to the conclusion, therefore, since he had taken the time and trouble to explain it to me, that this was very much in the forefront of party politics, and this was clearly, from a doctrinal point of view, the aim of the Croats in that particular area of which he was representing the head of the political party, and I was frankly concerned. We then moved on to discuss his attitude towards Muslim people where he stated that the population of the Muslims was increasing and he showed me statistical charts to prove that the Muslim population would increase and the Croat and Serb population in Bosnia would diminish. He then further showed me examples of what he felt were unacceptable behaviour by Muslims in their domination of villages with minarets, their loud and noisy prayers. We then further went on to discuss an individual. I stated, "What about the people you have grown up with, the people you went to school with here in Vitez?" And I said, "Presumably you went to school with people, you were at university in Sarajevo, as many of your countrymen were, with other ethnic nations, and you have lived in Vitez afterwards and now you hate all these people." And he said: "Absolutely. I cannot live with them." And I was again disturbed. But I then went back to a meeting I had had in Vitez, the Vitez headquarters, the same headquarters, on the 9th of May, my first meeting, where I had met Commander Blaskic and a man called Dario Kordic, and we were discussing at that meeting the events of Ahmici, and it occurred to me, here was the fulfilment of that policy, the policy of forcible movement of individuals which had been expounded by Anto Valenta, had now been enacted in the form of Croats, HVO, cleaning out, using armed forces, a village, Ahmici, and that is why I said earlier there was this complete change in what was going on, the sea change, this huge hostility. An army had moved and killed Muslims. The doctrine was there by Anto Valenta, I assumed that Dario Kordic was a politician, the next level down, and that policy and doctrine had then been put into place by the military in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us stay with that -- those two events, if we may, for one moment, Brigadier, and talk a little bit -- and we will talk about it later on -- but let us talk a little bit about this meeting on the 9th that you had with Dario Kordic and Blaskic wherein the events of Ahmici were discussed. Could you tell the President and Judge Riad people that you recall that were there, what Blaskic said, what you said, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I can recall at the meeting, the 9th, it was the first meeting I had, I believe, with Commander Blaskic. I was not running the meeting in that Colonel Stewart at that stage was still in command. We sat down. The first things Colonel Stewart did were to complain about the events of Ahmici and ask questions as to why and how HVO soldiers were seen marching off some 150 Muslims, why Muslims were now in gaol in Vitez and being detained against their will, and what exactly was going on, and what was the explanation of these events? The explanation of these events which I heard at that time was that either --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From whom? From whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Blaskic. Was either it had been done by Muslim extremists who had somehow come into the Vitez pocket and committed this event and disappeared in the night on their own people or indeed Muslim armed forces from the BiH or, finally, by Muslims dressed in HVO uniform, were the three reasons given. I'm sorry, I should refresh that. The three reasons given were Serb extremists, Muslims who had infiltrated the pocket, or Muslims dressed in HVO uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you think about that and what did you say, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I sat at the background and thought to myself: Well, how is it possible for Muslims at this stage of what was going on in Central Bosnia to commit a full-scale military attack on a village which effectively resulted in opening a second front for their military operation when, at the same time, they were desperately defending against the Serbs? Also, would they really go and kill some 97 people from their own race? I thought that explanation was pretty unlikely. As to the infiltration of the Serbs to do it, this was plainly and completely, absolutely ludicrous, and I dismissed that out of hand. As for the insinuation that it had been done by Muslims dressed in HVO uniforms, the only thing I conclude from that was that there was an acknowledgement that HVO uniforms were on the spot in Ahmici and had been there; otherwise, why mention the HVO uniforms? Frankly, all three reasons I found ridiculous, and I said so. I said, "This is just impossible." I also stated at that meeting that if the HVO wished to have any credibility with the International Community, they should and must convene a formal investigation and show the world who had done this crime. And if their reasons and the statements as to who had done it were correct, then we should all be able to see them. This was agreed. I believe it had been agreed previously between Colonel Stewart and Commander Blaskic, and a date of the 25th of May was set for the conclusion of this investigation to be published. To my knowledge, that has never been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, a couple of questions based on what you just said. Did Blaskic say anything about whether or not his troops, the HVO troops, were involved or not involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said his troops were not involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you follow up with a question and ask him anything concerning that denial in light of the information you had in your possession concerning the civilians being marched down the street by HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We followed it up in that I said, you know, "Why are you HVO troops in the area? If it wasn't HVO troops, who was it?" And he went back to the line of these three possibilities: extremists out of control was often-used as an excuse, "Extremists in my area who are not under my control." Which I found again surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier -- and part of my directness in this question, did you conclude that the Defendant was lying to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. There was no other conclusion. He was lying. And the problem was, it wasn't even a clever lie. It was very naive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you the second portion of Exhibit 380. Mr. President and Judge Riad, we're moving to the second translated paragraph in 380 which is taken from the last paragraph of the Bosnian-Serbo-Croatian version, and this has likewise been translated into French and English. Could you read that question and that answer, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question to Commander Blaskic runs as follows: "You investigated a crime in Ahmici. What is the result of the investigation so far?" The reply from Commander Blaskic was: "The investigation is still in progress. Information is being gathered. In any case, this is a well-planned scenario in which Muslim forces wanted once again to cast a blemish on units of the HVO before the world community. After the crimes that Muslim forces committed in the areas around the Croatian villages of Lasva, Ducina (phoen), Gusti Grab and other villages in Busovaca municipality, the case of Ahmici was staged and skilfully shown to foreign reporters and the EC Observer Commission with the assistance of the Commander of the British battalion at that time, Bob Stewart. So far, we are certain that the crime was committed by members of the HOS, the Croatian defence force in Zenica, which was mostly Muslim and parts of the Muslim forces of the MLS, the Muslim defence force, and I have already said that the investigation is continuing. "It is certain that the HVO does not stand behind the crime that others desire to attribute to us. However, I want to say that a much greater crime is being skilfully concealed. Muslim forces shot to death more than 40 civilians, mostly women and children, back in the beginning of June in the village of Meliha, Travnik municipality. We have not been allowed to this day, nor has the UNHCR --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want to excuse you. Please go more slowly. The interpreters are having a great deal of difficulty following you if you read it. If they don't have the text with them, I could give it to them. I do have the translation here. Nevertheless, I would ask that you go a little bit more slowly so that it can make the work of the interpreters a little easier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. I will start again with the last sentence of the first page. "The Muslim forces shot to death more than 40 civilians, mostly women and children, back at the beginning of June in the village of Melina, Travnik municipality. We have not been allowed to this day, nor has the UNHCR or the International Red Cross or the European Observer Commission to look around the area and perform an exhumation of the bodies. That was a collective execution in front of other Croats who had to dig the grave for those killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, this article, published in the 5 October, 1993 edition of Danas, basically blames the Muslims for killing their own people once again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what it insinuates, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What do you think about that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I disagree entirely. I mean, it is a continuation of the same first lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's move on at this juncture and move to another area, and I'd like to talk, if you can, about your experiences, your observations, and what you can tell the Court about Blaskic's command given your experiences with him, and if you could give the Court an idea of approximately how often you saw the Defendant so we have some framework upon which you base your comments that you are about to give.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Commander Blaskic at regular intervals throughout the seven months I was in Bosnia. I didn't always rush to see him, but we saved my meetings for what I thought were important events of discussion, rather than running across and speaking every few days. So it was about a week to ten days apart, our meetings. Of course, we were actually very close together because the area, the whole area of the Vitez pocket, at that stage was very small, and it was a matter of minutes, about ten minutes for me to move down to his headquarters as I wished. As for his status as a commander, it was quite clear to me that he was very much the commander. He had all the trappings of command. He had a large headquarters which was well equipped with staff. He had deputy commanders; he had liaison officers. There were communications in his headquarters. He told me, as I've already mentioned, that he was the commander. Of course, he also received great recognition afterwards as the commander of that Vitez pocket by his promotion and he was clearly a successful and capable commander. He had been a captain, I believe, in the Yugoslav National Army, a regular soldier, and therefore he had a full education in tactics, the Geneva Convention, and the rules and regulations of war, how to plan operations, how to conduct them. He was a professional soldier throughout. I should add that others in the area also saw him very much as the commander and the one who had influence and control. Members of the UNHCR, the international committee of the Red Cross, the various aid agencies in the area and the U.N. themselves, civil affairs and others, would call in and see Commander Blaskic at his headquarters because he was the one who was exercising command in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to that last part about the exercise of his command. Can you talk a little bit about the exercise of that command and the communications involved, the troop movements involved, what his mission was and how he conducted that mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His mission was to defend the Vitez pocket which he did very effectively. He exercised that command from the headquarters but he often moved out to inspect troops on the ground. There were occasions when I came to that headquarters where Commander Blaskic would be returning in his Land Rover dressed with his helmet and flak jacket on. He had clearly been out on the ground inspecting his front-lines to get a real feel for what was going on. He had also, on occasion, moved to Kiseljak. Indeed, I had taken him once to a meeting with other HVO commanders. He had perhaps, in the entire seven months, two or three absences from the Vitez pocket where he moved out. I was not sure how he moved out but I was aware there was a helicopter. He was able to communicate with that helicopter, clearly, to arrange its arrival and departure. That came from a considerable distance away, we believe, from the area of Prozor, well to the south. So he could call it forward and move it and arrange visits as required, which requires a fair amount of communications equipment. He also had fax machines and access to the local telephone network and he would send us faxes in my headquarters in Vitez. He had knowledge of events outside of his own pocket, and on one occasion he gave me a list of villages in the Vares area which had been overrun by the Muslim BiH forces. That list was fairly complete, and obviously he had the intelligence network available to gather such information across his command. As far as I'm aware, he also had satellite communications, motorola, and I have already mentioned the liaison officers. In all, I would say it was quite clear to me he was a commander exercising command, issuing orders, controlling events as and when required in the classic style of any military commander operating a large headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me ask a question of you, Brigadier, based on what you just said. You noted that Blaskic was conducting himself in the Defence of the Vitez pocket. Is it essential in such a defence or was it essential in such a defence that a commander, such as Blaskic, know what's happening within that pocket, and I mean everywhere in that pocket and, if so, why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is absolutely vital that a commander, a military commander, knows exactly what's happening particularly in defence. The shape of the Vitez pocket was such that there was a spinal road running down the middle from the Novi Travnik T-junction down through Vitez to Busovaca. It was on that road that the movement of reserves could take place. The defence was structured in that there were soldiers who were committed to territorial areas, mainly because I think they lived there and therefore they could do ten days on the front-line and ten days off. That was the framework of defence which held the perimeter of the pocket. The spinal road down the middle was used to shuttle the troops, the reserves, as quickly as possible. The defence rested on the basis that attacks on foot could only advance at the speed of walking, whereas the reserves could be moved by bus, truck or lorry, and therefore they could quickly move to put out the fire, as it were. It is exactly the same situation from a military point of view that existed in the First World War, where attacks on foot by the soldiers were easily stopped and nipped in the bud because trains brought in reinforcements at a much quicker speed. To operate that sort of defence, firstly, there must be one commander; secondly, he must have everything in that area directly under his command, and he must have an adequate information and communication system in order to be able to operate that defence. I have to say that Commander Blaskic operated that defence superbly because he had all of those ingredients, and that is how he was able to defend that pocket with great skill throughout those seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As a subset of what you just mentioned, would it be essential for a commander such as Blaskic to be aware of where his defensive positions were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was and he often, in our discussions, showed me a map where he thought the likely attacks were going to come in, and recorded on that map were details of his front-line trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So he indicated to you that he knew that there were trenches at various locations about the pocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very much so. The symbols on the map indicated there was a large and extensive trench network around that pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Brigadier, he knew what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to the next area of our discussion, Brigadier, which has to do with Blaskic's obligations as a commander and his meeting those obligations and his failure to meet those obligations based on your experiences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already spoken about the value of an independent investigation, and there were a number of events during this time in command that I think warranted investigation, the first being Ahmici. As I've already said, we were promised the results of an investigation by the 25th of May, and to date they don't appear to have been published or announced anywhere. As I've already said, my conclusion from Ahmici, that was the doctrine and the politics of the area being put into effect. The next event of interest was when a Muslim convoy moved through my area in early June. As far as I'm aware, there were papers of agreement between Muslims and Croat military, the HVO, that this convoy comprising a large number of vehicles, of trucks, should be allowed through the area unmolested. There was a serious incident where the convoy was stopped as it came into the Vitez pocket, I believe, by HVO police who stopped it and HVO soldiers. The convoy was then looted and to the extent that some of the drivers were pulled out and we believe that eight drivers were actually shot and killed on that convoy as it came through. Now, again, no action was taken to investigate that incident whatsoever. Here were people killed and yet nobody bothered to investigate it. Why did they not bother to investigate it? Well, presumably, they didn't want anyone to know what the truth was. And it was all very well denying what had happened, but it was quite clear what had happened and most of it was witnessed by my own troops and is on the record, and I believe also there are video clips to substantiate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before you move to the next incident, if we can, Mr. President and Judge Riad, if we can move to the video clip. That is with the video room and I believe that would be Exhibit 381 at this juncture, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the source of these video clips, Mr. President, these are video clips that come from the BBC, some that were shown on the air and some that were rushes or outtakes that were likewise given to the Office of the Prosecutor by the BBC. If we could dim the lights and play this particular video segment. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you just rewind that back? Can you go back to the beginning, please? Just play it from the beginning. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, there's an individual in that, if we can just roll it a couple of more frames, being beaten by soldiers; is that right, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we move it a couple of more frames to the chap in the back, there is an individual, a military policeman, there as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These were, to your knowledge, HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the HVO badge on the arm of the military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop right there. In the background where all the shooting is going on, there are soldiers in uniform in the background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and some have the white cross belts of HVO police on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is one of your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is Corporal Neil Bolman, yes. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop again. There is yet again another soldier in the back in camouflage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very clearly you can see the white soldier brassard of an HVO military policeman. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop again. Again, troops in the background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop there. Is that one of the drivers shot in his truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was one of the drivers from the Muslim convoy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, that's Corporal Bolman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's Corporal Bolman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, stop there. What is going on here, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's HVO soldiers looting the vehicles belonging to the convoy. The convoy not only had trucks in it but also some cars full of possessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop there. You mentioned during the commentary that some of the trucks were taken to the quarry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you explain this video clip and we can continue on here with this video clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This video clip shows the quarry at Vitez where a number of the buses and trucks were taken to be looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was not the quarry a location where the HVO had a station there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. In this particular event, you said eight people were killed; you observed soldiers looting. To your knowledge, did the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone, the defendant, ever do anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, sir, there was no investigation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you conclude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they didn't want an investigation because the investigation would prove who had done it, and the people who had done it, quite clearly as has been shown on the video and witnessed by my soldiers, were HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This particular event, Brigadier, based on you being on the ground and seeing this, who is directing this operation and what was the participation of the defendant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The operation, I believe, was directed by Dario Kordic. The reason it was being directed by Dario Kordic is that he was the political leader of that area and at that stage, the Croat forces were very much on the back foot. The pocket had been sealed off from the outside world. They were running short of food and Dario Kordic had decided that this convoy, which was agreed would go through, he would let soldiers and the population take food and supplies off that convoy. If you like, it was a percentage cut to allow it to go through. That wasn't published as an agreement but it is the only thing that I could conclude that he had decided they would be allowed to remove a certain amount of that convoy and he would judge the risk involved. Therefore, it was politically motivated, but as with everything else, you have a political decision and you require troops and forces to plan and conduct the operation. Now, the planning and conduct would need to be detailed. You would need to decide where to stop vehicles, where to cut them out, and it was quite apparent as that convoy came through there had been a detailed plan, we will stop them here, we will loot them here, we will let those vehicles through to another point on the Vitez bypass where we can stop them and control them and cut them out to various parts of Vitez. Trucks were systematically moved. That's a plan you can't dream up as a politician. You need someone who is an expert in the planning and control. The people in the Vitez area who were the experts of planning, control, organisation and operations were the military and therefore it had to have the involvement of HVO forces, otherwise the plan simply wouldn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No investigation in Ahmici, no investigation with the looting and the killing of the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No investigation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you give us a date approximately of the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we go to the next point, Brigadier, I would like to show you a document, and it is this particular document with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Claudius, it is this document with the date of 30 June on the letterhead, a document of then Colonel Duncan.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is 382.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, the events of the Convoy of Joy, approximately 10th or 11th of June 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, around early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I show you a letter dated 30 June, 1993 which has your signature line at the bottom of that page. Do you recognise that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is a letter I wrote to Commander Blaskic. His name and appointment are on the top left hand corner of that letter. It concerned a launch or strike of a rocket launcher on my base in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell the judges about that. What happened? What the ultimate result was and give us the timing involved in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see from the letter that an incident occurred at my headquarters on the 27th of June and that incident was the firing of an explosive missile into my base where my soldiers were stationed. Naturally, I was extremely irritated, which is an understatement. I was absolutely furious. My soldiers had been deliberately fired at, as far as I was concerned. I put a very speedy complaint directly to Commander Blaskic about it. You can see that I have praised the speed and efficiency on which he did it because I refer at reference A, which is just above paragraph 1, to the HVO third operational zone letter dated the 29th of June '93, which was his reply, which told me that he had investigated the incident, he had discovered that it was one of his soldiers who was responsible. The investigation was fully complete. The soldier had been put on trial, had been found guilty and was now incarcerated in Busovaca prison. Now, that whole process had taken approximately two days. An investigation had been launched, come to a conclusion, an action had been taken. I found it rather surprising that this investigation could be done so quickly when others, either were not initiated or came to no conclusion or were just ignored. This to me demonstrated that Commander Blaskic had the structure, the orders and the discipline system necessary to conduct very swiftly and efficiently investigations if he so wished. If he didn't wish to conduct an investigation, clearly it hadn't been done in the case of Ahmici and the Convoy of Joy. In this case, I had a clear demonstration, that actually, as a commander he could do it if he wanted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He could do it if he wanted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's move to the tragic events of five days later and the question of whether or not Blaskic wanted to do anything about what happened five days later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five days later, and the date will be with me for some time, it was the 5th of July, my interpreter, my personal interpreter was shot dead on the steps of her house in my camp. She was shot by an HVO sniper from the HVO lines across the road. That was entirely clear to me. I think it was clear to everybody in the camp. She was shot, I believe, because she had been Colonel Stewart's personal interpreter and she had attended meetings with Colonel Stewart. She knew what was going on. She was a clear link between the past and the present and a very useful source of advice to me. She was shot because she was easily identifiable. She was a very tall, striking Bosnian Serb. She wasn't shot because she was a Bosnian Serb. She was shot because she was useful to me and it was a distinct poke at me, to get at me, and it was distressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move on to that, if we can move to the next clip, which shows exactly, Mr. President and Judge Riad, who this woman was, and if we can move to the next clip which is Exhibit 383? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, this is from the BBC, Mr. President. Stop right there. Is Dobrilla in that frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the left of the frame, you can very clearly see wearing the blue helmet, a tall girl whose name is Dobrilla Kalava.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, is Dobrilla in that frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she's on the right of the frame there walking down with Colonel Stewart. There you can see her again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: She is likewise the woman translating in that clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this last clip of her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This last clip shows her being moved on a stretcher from the place where she was shot. She had been given immediate first aid for her severe gunshot wound to the head. She is now being moved out. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point, Brigadier, at the time of that clip, Dobrilla Kalava is dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she was dead before she hit the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me put this last clip into some geographic frame of reference for the President and Judge Riad and if we can move to Exhibit 384 which is an enlargement of a portion of Exhibit 182, the map with the three colourings?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's 384.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can put that on the ELMO, Claudius, please? Now, Brigadier, this is an enlargement of Exhibit 172. Can you take us through the particular coloured areas and tell the court what they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could start with this large blue area, that is the perimeter of the British base in Vitez. This area is the hill behind Grbavica area and the main road running through is the main road coming from Novi Travnik in the south and on to Vitez in the north. What is shown on this slide is the firstly of that British base area, and inside that British base, ringed by the yellow circle, is the house where Dobrilla was shot, and then the orange lozenge there is the area on the other side of the road from whence the shooting came. I should say that this road actually marked the front-line down there between the Muslim forces on this side and the Croat forces on the right-hand side, but it was quite clear to us that the shot had come from across the road from houses which had been occupied by Croat forces for some two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By HVO forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This took place on the 5th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Five days after you complimented Judge Blaskic (sic) on his expeditious investigation of this launch into your camp that took place on the 27th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Colonel Blaskic, on the 27th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the HVO investigate this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military policeman were sent down to talk to us. There was an investigation. It came to the conclusion that somehow a Muslim had infiltrated across the road, occupied houses that were then occupied by HVO soldiers, deliberately shot Dobrilla and then clearly moved himself back across the front-line and escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you think of that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think to say that was unlikely would be an understatement. It was, again, almost ludicrous and naive to suggest something like that. I mean, here was an investigation suggesting to my officers and myself something that patently wasn't true. It was a complete lie. Not only was it a small lie, it was such a huge and such an elaborate lie, it was unbelievable anyone could suggest that. And producing investigations which came up with such ridiculous solutions undermined the whole system. What is the point? It was a complete waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there any other events after the murder of Dobrilla Kalava which called into question the actions of Blaskic in his failure to meet his obligations as a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one other murder of a UNHCR official called Boris. He was the driver in a UNHCR vehicle. The vehicle was moving in the area of Stari Vitez and a single round from a 12.7 millimetre machine gun penetrated his armoured vehicle and went straight through him and killed him on the spot. Again, we asked for an investigation of this. There was no investigation. The reason there was no investigation is we knew that the HVO had shot him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the murder of this driver Boris that took place on the 14th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, to give the court a frame of reference concerning this particular event, can we turn our attention to Exhibit 385, Mr. Dubuisson, which is this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, we started a little bit earlier this morning. Perhaps, if you don't mind, we could take a break now, 20 minutes, and then resume at 11.35. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, before we move to the map that's on the ELMO, 385, I neglected to ask you a couple of questions concerning the orders of battle, Exhibits 378 and 379. The question I neglected to ask is the fact that within these orders of battle, there is no specific designation for the military police. Is there some reason for that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We would not normally show units such as military police or other units who are supporting the main effort. We would merely show the main units themselves; and therefore, they wouldn't -- on an order of battle such as we produced, we don't put them on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned during your testimony this morning that you took Blaskic to Kiseljak on the 29th of May of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- I'm not sure I mentioned it this morning, but I certainly was ordered by BHC command in Kiseljak to move Commander Blaskic to a meeting at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, was that a meeting that was at the U.N. headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a meeting -- it was to be a meeting at the U.N. headquarters, yes, but the understanding was that after that meeting, the HVO commanders would be allowed some time before they were required to return to their various locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the HVO commanders take that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What, in fact, happened was, we arrived at the meeting, and very little business to do with the U.N. was done at all. The meeting was concluded very quickly. And then the HVO commanders moved off with Petkovic, their commander, away, and I saw them about three hours later when they got a lift back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which HVO commanders are you talking about met with General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly Commander Blaskic, Rajic, and other brigade commander level commanders in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After that meeting, did you see a relationship between the HVO and the Bosnian Serb army develop in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a considerable change after that meeting which was on the 29th of May. After that, Croat civilians were able to move across front-lines into Serb territory, particularly in the area of Travnik, where they moved off to the west and then came back in lower down in Herceg-Bosna, and also in the area of Zepce, where Croats were working, and I think HVO were working with the Serb army against the Muslims, and then also in the Vares area where there was certainly cooperation, we believe, between Serb and Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One other subject area which didn't come up this morning which I'd like to ask you about and has to do with Prozor. Brigadier, you went through Prozor on occasion during your tour. On any occasion during your tour did you see HV troops, troops from the Republic of Croatia, present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw HV artillery troops and guns in the area of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately what time of year was this, if you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the middle of the year. I couldn't specify it exactly. But certainly I have personally seen HV soldiers in the area of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During your tour in 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my tour in '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us return back to where we left off before the break, and we had finished talking about the murder of Dobrilla Kalava, and I believe you were about to discuss or had discussed the killing of the UNHCR driver, Boris, on the 14th of August of 1993, and I believe we have on the -- we had it on the ELMO. We're about to move to this particular map, Mr. President, Exhibit 385. Now, Brigadier, pursuant to your instructions, did members of British battalion conduct an investigation concerning this shooting of this UNHCR driver and did they determine the firing point and who controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a result of Boris's shooting, we recovered the vehicle back to our camp in Vitez, and we then examined the entry and exit holes of the bullet; and from the position in the road that the vehicle was on, it was apparent that the firing point came from this village called Krvenija (phoen), I think it's called, it's marked on the map, it's a very simple blob of orange there, that was a village that was occupied at the time by HVO troops, and we believe it was the firing point from which they would fire down into Stari Vitez, and this is the road outside Stari Vitez which is where Boris was killed. I should add that Boris was a driver for the UNHCR. It was in the interests of the Muslims to get the UNHCR into Stari Vitez in order to get aid. It would be highly unlikely that they would wish to shoot somebody who was bringing them aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, how large a calibre of this round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's 12.7, I believe, millimetres, which is a very large round, an armour-piercing round.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, did you discuss the killing of Boris with the Defendant Blaskic and, if so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said categorically that the HVO hadn't done it, it had been done by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you think of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's another statement which was patently a lie. It's just simply not true. As I've said, there was no reason for the Muslims to shoot a white vehicle which was going to bring them aid, or organised to bring aid in, a well-known vehicle. It's the UNHCR vehicle that moved around the area. There was no reason for anyone else except HVO to shoot. Certainly it came from their lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's continue on, Brigadier, and talk about any other events that you wish to discuss with the Court concerning the Defendant Blaskic's failure to meet his obligations as a commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are a number of events which I consider as a commander, Commander Blaskic, failed to act on a direction he was given. Throughout the period I was there, there were a number of prisoners held by the Croats, and there were repeated requests from the International Committee of the Red Cross, from the European monitoring teams, and from the United Nations to release prisoners. Clearly, these prisoners weren't released because we kept finding them throughout the seven months I was there; and when we found them, of course, they were released. But there was a failure to comply with instructions and requests throughout the period to release prisoners. More specifically, I think, during the period where I convened joint military committees between the Bosnian Muslim army and the Croat Bosnian army, the HVO, there were a number of decisions which we took at those meetings which are agreed by both commanders, that is by -- in the main by Enver Hadzihasanovic for the BiH and by Tihomir Blaskic for the HVO, agreement of action which we had taken which clearly wasn't taken by the HVO, and we could perhaps outline those now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could move to the next four exhibits, and they are the reports on the meeting of the joint command that were drafted by you, Brigadier? We are preparing French copies of these, Mr. President. They have not been finalised as of yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 386 for the document of 19 June. 387 for the 21st of June. 388 for the 20th (sic) of June. 389 for the one that has no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, 388 was identified as the 20th of June. The transcript has been changed to the 24th. Could I ask the registrar: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe my colleague is correct. 388 should read the 24th of June, 1993. It is written in there, and it's a little difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You can continue with the examination-in-chief starting with that document, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, these are documents that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you take us through these particular meetings of the joint command and what do we have before us, the record of decisions, and can you explain, based on this, what was discussed and what the problems were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. These four documents represent the output of four meetings I had between the BiH and the HVO in Vitez on the dates as shown. I would draw your attention to the third page of the document, of the first document, and I believe that is similar on the others, which gives a distribution of those who received that document, and you can see it runs Colonel Blaskic, Colonel Filipovic, Colonel Hadzihasanovic, Karic, Merdan, Nakic, Siber Totic, which was the main hierarchy of both HVO and BiH at that time. So they had personal copies. The important thing about these documents is that they record the decisions that were agreed between the two commanders, and I don't wish to go through the documents in detail. I would wish to draw your attention to certain paragraphs, if I may? First, paragraph 4(a), which is halfway down the first page of the first document, where --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
