utterances.text: At either the first or the second place where the Convoy of Joy was stopped, did your men, the men of UNPROFOR, use force to try and clear the crowd or clear the civilians -- excuse me, or clear soldiers away, et cetera? Did they fire upon anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We fired at the first location, subsequent to the killing of the eight Muslims, because clearly at this stage, although our mandate didn't allow us to get involved with the movement of this convoy because it was not a U.N. convoy, when life was placed at risk, we were then empowered to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm not being critical in the least, but after firing or as a result of firing, were any persons wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were persons wounded within the area of the Vitez pocket. I believe two people were killed by my soldiers who fired at them because they had fired first, and these were HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever told anything more whether these were local soldiers from the village or villages adjacent to where the convoy had stopped, or were they from some other location and thus may have been sent in to that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that the two soldiers who were killed were locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You commented critically with respect to Colonel Blaskic and said there was no investigation, to your knowledge, of the events surrounding the Convoy of Joy. Did you write to him and ask him to investigate the deaths of the Muslim drivers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not write to him, no. I asked him to investigate at one of our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, though, that it's not something you pressed with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How often does one have to ask? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, did you ask only once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked twice, I would say. Certainly no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was he present at the first location where the convoy was stopped, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was ever given a copy of the BBC broadcast or outtakes that have been shown here in court? Did you give him a copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't give him a copy, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant, I think you said Bulmer of your force, did he make a report concerning his observations in and around Puticevo, the first location where the convoy was stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Corporal Bulmer was speaking to me on the radio about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you give Colonel Blaskic a copy of Corporal Bulmer's report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This was all on the 10th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When did Travnik fall? That is, when did the HVO lose Travnik? Was that about two days later, Brigadier, the 12th of June, 1993, 12th or 14th, within a few days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was either slightly before or slightly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the fall of Travnik caused the exodus of in excess of 10.000 refugees, Croat refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, but an awful lot of them went across the border with the Serbs. They went west, not east.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did some of them come back around to Vitez or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came back into Herceg-Bosna down in the south, I believe. That wasn't my area. I don't know. Certainly I can say that some people from Travnik came to the east, but a lot walked across the border into Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that if Colonel Blaskic gave the order for the HVO soldiers present at the Vitez T-junction to stop and loot the convoy, that those soldiers would have followed an order from him to stop doing so; do you agree with that general proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume if Colonel Blaskic had given an order, yes, that is a reasonable supposition to make, that if he gives an order, his soldiers would follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have stated your belief that Dario Kordic directed these activities against the Convoy of Joy. Do you have any specific information, if, in fact, it's true that he directed it, how he implemented his plan or direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my belief that this particular event was orchestrated by Dario Kordic, but he would clearly had to involved somebody who could plan and decide the best places to loot the convoy. It was my belief that there was an arrangement between the Croats, Petkovic, who was there and had come and visited just the day before and was still there at the time, that some arrangement whereby a cut could be taken out of this convoy by the people on the ground. That was an arrangement. It was convenient for Kordic, who was the politician, to marshal the people because, if you like, Kordic commanded the people. It was Commander Blaskic's job to keep his command on his own troops, including the military police who were under his command. Those police transgressed and did not assist. Now, they just sat by and watched. Whether they were on or off duty, they are still subject, I believe, to a military code.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were the soldiers in uniform at the Vitez T-junction where the Convoy of Joy was stopped, HVO military policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that Colonel Blaskic told you on a regular basis that he was not able to control the thousands of displaced persons within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did. I also reminded him on a regular basis that it was his responsibility to control the military which he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were aware that the control of displaced persons in Vitez was the responsibility of the local mayor and the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 382 could be provided to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Brigadier, this pertains to the rocket incident whereby a rocket of some sort entered your camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have related that Colonel Blaskic informed you that an investigation had occurred and this is your reply letter, I believe; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is thanking him for his very prompt response to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn who within the HVO had investigated this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. As far as I was concerned, it was a matter for the HVO to do and I wouldn't have asked Commander Blaskic who had investigated it specifically. That was his business. It was enough for him to tell me, in his response, that he had taken swift action and as a result of which somebody was now incarcerated in Busovaca jail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would it be normal for the military police to investigate incidents of a criminal nature within a military organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be normal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you held the HVO military police in extremely low regard, you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I find that a strange remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then let me help you. Page 4 of your statement, the first full paragraph, is it correct what you said in this statement as follows and I quote: "The local HVO police force would routinely steal any equipment they could get their hands on and were generally little better than uniformed thugs." Is that your statement and is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you were referring to the HVO military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but may I just point something out?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You can point out anything you wish, Brigadier. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to point out, if I can make a point, that these were my impressions gained at that time as the result of specific incidents. We are talking about a snapshot when I had that opinion. Events later on may have changed my opinion. If you take individual incidents about which I was extremely annoyed, then I would have had an opinion. For example, I may have written down that they are a bunch of thugs after they had stolen one of the UNHCR vehicles. But on occasions, clearly the military police had followed up later on and done a very thorough investigation somewhere. So if you keep taking snapshots out, I think it gives a false impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This statement was given on the 16th of April 1997; correct? Do you see that on the last page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you name any incidents involving the HVO military police that occurred after the 16th of April, 1997 that might have changed the opinion you gave on page 4 of your statement which I've already read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know -- I'm sorry, I can't reply directly to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were out of the theatre; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was obviously out of the theatre. All I'm saying is that since I have left the theatre and been able to look at the entire situation that was involved there, I have been able to see, as opposed to just a series of incidents, a better -- I've been able to see events in contrast and balance them more. At the moment when I was there at the time, I was reacting to individual events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The statement that I read from was given in 1997, not at the moment when you were in the theatre; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, and I had done a little analysis of what had happened in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Ahmici, is it fair to say you were critical of Colonel Blaskic for not ordering an investigation into the events in Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Has the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor told you that he did order an investigation into the events in Ahmici or did they fail to tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware he had ordered an investigation. I was also aware that investigation was to have been concluded by the 25th of May. To my knowledge, it has yet to be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you learned otherwise, might that change your opinion with respect to your views of whether Colonel Blaskic discharged his obligations as a commander with respect to investigating events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There would be a requirement of more than just completing the investigation. If the investigation had been completed and then came out with the same set of comments as to what had happened, which were clearly false, then the investigation, in my mind, would have been worthless.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You would have expected him under those circumstances to order a further investigation, a better investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you've just asked the witness whether there are any other elements. Let's not go around the difficulty. If there are any -- we're speculating now about knowing whether the witness's opinion would change if such and such happened. Let's not speculate that way, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I just state that it would be the duty of a military commander if he was not satisfied that the outcome of an investigation was realistic to order a re-investigation or even place it into somebody else's hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If he did that, might your testimony change on this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are, I think with respect, sir, in the realms of speculation again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But you would agree you don't have complete information on this issue; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your testimony from personal information --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. The answer is the answer. We're in the area of speculation. If counsel has got a report of the investigation that Blaskic did, show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has the report. He obviously didn't show it to the witness and elicited a professional opinion that our client failed to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let's be calm. Mr. Hayman, three times now you're asking the witness whether his mind would change if he had other elements. Perhaps it would, perhaps it wouldn't, but this is the third time now that you're asking the same question. So either there are additional elements that would supplement this embryonic type of investigation which has been done, but to say to the witness, "Would you change if this and that happened," no, please move on to another question, unless you have specific elements that you're going to mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour. The point I'm making is that the Prosecutor has two orders for investigations into Ahmici. They didn't show this witness either one of them and yet they elicited the opinion testimony which they elicited. That's my only point. I'll move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to counsel's specious arguments in this regard. Defence counsel should ask the witness whether or not the Office of the Prosecutor showed him any documents over the past couple of days upon which that investigation was ordered by Blaskic. Ask the witness the question and see what the witness answers, as opposed to taking critical comments about the Office of the Prosecutor, but we haven't had that question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We did have that question, Mr. President. It's in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ask the question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It was asked and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Are there additional elements? Were there other investigations? I can ask this under Rule 98 that there were additional investigations into the Ahmici incidents by the defendant. That's the question. I'm asking the question now. Were there any additional elements? I, the judge, am asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have no results of any investigation. What we have in our possession is the letter that counsel was waving around that I showed to Brigadier Duncan, the letter of the 10th, in which the results were supposed to be handed up on the 25th of May of 1993. That is what was discussed. The results of this investigation by the defendant?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel has two orders from our client ordering investigations into Ahmici and he is defrauding the court in stating otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, please, please, the particular order that the witness was just talking about that ordered the results on the 25th of May which was an order that was given out the day after Brigadier Duncan's meeting on the 9th was discussed with the brigadier. The Defence counsel doesn't want to ask him because he doesn't like the answer, and to cast dispersions on the Office of the Prosecutor that it's trying to mislead this court is improper and Defence counsel knows it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Oh, you're both speaking so quickly that the interpreters are having a lot of difficulty following you and interpreting what you're saying which makes it even more difficult. Therefore, I will ask you again. Yes or no, were there additional investigations that were conducted by the accused about Ahmici beyond the initial investigation, that's the first question, of the 25th. That's the question I would like to ask you. Mr. Prosecutor, do you know of any additional investigations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We know of no subsequent investigation after Blaskic's order with the redactions on it that were provided to us on the 10th upon which to give results by the 25th of May of 1993. That is the last that we know of the Ahmici investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Does this correspond with your idea, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, move to another question now because I don't see how we can go on endlessly discussing what the witness would have thought about an investigation which didn't take place. However, apparently if there were additional investigations, if there were, then the Tribunal would reconsider its position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There is a second order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Brigadier, you've never seen the second order to further investigate Ahmici from our client, Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness has answered he did not see a second order. Did you see another one, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Inaudible).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. If you have a second order, Mr. Hayman, you have to produce it and then, if necessary, we will have the witness come back. This is the second time this morning we have said we may have to bring this witness back, although we will try not to have to do that. Mr. Hayman, the incident is closed. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have spoken of Colonel Blaskic's duties as being those of defending the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, did the BiH army admit to you that it held as a goal cutting the Vitez/Busovaca enclave into a number of pieces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And they told you, in fact, that they thought they would achieve that goal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were very confident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They, in fact, tried to achieve that goal repeatedly during your tour; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to show you a series of reports from your unit, and I'm going to give you five of them and first ask you just to look at them and tell us if you can authenticate them as reports of your unit. I have five different documents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If they could be numbered in order as the next Defence exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D-136.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While they are being labelled, Brigadier, if you could look to them with an eye towards telling us whether or not they are MILINFOSUMS which have been heavily redacted but, nonetheless, were generated by the Prince of Wales own?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take as long as you need, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could the registrar correlate the exhibit numbers with the dates while we're waiting for the witness to complete his review.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have scanned through them, yes, and they have the appearance of being extracts, obviously taken out of context, which slightly concerns me because of what other information may have been on the page. And, therefore, you have taken something in isolation of any other comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I share your concern.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also, some of the abbreviations are unusual in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I give them to you in the same form that we received them from the Prosecutor, Brigadier. If I could do better, I would. Let me ask you to turn your attention to the extract that's dated 6 September, 1993. I hate to burden you; can you tell us what number has been assigned to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is Exhibit D-136.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. Let me read to you the comment so we can have it translated and then I will ask you about the comment. The comment appears in the middle of the front page: "Comment: The immediate BiH objective in this area is to capture Zabilje. This will then ultimately allow their forces to push further south in order to cut the HVO MSR, main supply route, which runs west to east through GR SQ 1995. As has been reported previously, it is the BiH long-term aim to divide the Novi Travnik/Vitez/Busovaca/Croat enclave into a number of smaller isolated pockets. End comment." First of all, Brigadier, is that correct? Do you agree with the comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it seems an entirely reasonable comment for somebody to make. It outlines the BiH ambitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, can you help us, Zabilje, is that to the north, north-west of the Stari Bila feature and thus also to the north, north-west of the Grbavica feature above the BRITBAT camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I don't know without having a look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. The court has those maps in evidence so we needn't belabour the point. Let me ask you to turn your attention to the MILINFOSUM extract dated 28 September, '93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have that now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Exhibit number, if I may impose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's D-139.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is quite short. I'll read it in it's totality, Mr. President. "The level of activity in the area over the past few days and the fact that the Cajdras checkpoint is still manned by Seventh Muslim Brigade MP's in preventing access south towards Vitez suggests that these exchanges are more than mere routine. Darko Gelic, HVO operational zone Central Bosnia liaison officer to BRITBAT, claimed that the BiH launched activity noted today is possibly a continuation of this effort. It is noticeable that it is at this point that the Croat pocket is at its narrowest and, therefore, represents the easiest opportunity to cut the pocket in two. As yet, there are no indications as to any territorial changes." The comment ends: "A number of mortar rounds also fell in the centre of Vitez including three direct heads on the Croat Hospital at grid reference 244924, which killed two." With respect to the discussion of the BiH objective to cut or nip the pocket, is the contents of this MILINFOSUM consistent with your own knowledge and beliefs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Lastly on this subject, let me ask you to turn your attention to the extract dated 30 September 1993. First of all, there's an acronym in the second word, "NGO." Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, it means "non-governmental organisation." It is an acronym for an aid agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 3: "An NGO gained access to Kruscica on 29 September and noted that Fikret Cuskic, Commander 17th Slavna Krajina brigade, was in the village and had established a headquarters there. They also noted that there were a large amount of 17th Brigade soldiers in the village and that an HLS" -- can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means a helicopter landing site, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Had been laid out. BRITBAT G5 officer also noted in the office of Ramiz Dugalic, 3 corps security office, a map of the area which had arrows severing the Croat pocket at this point." Brigadier, was it known to you during your tour that one of the points at which the BiH army wished to cut the Vitez/Busovaca enclave was at the Kruscica Rijeka point just east of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was amongst a number of lines which we considered they might cut, but I should add that anything in a MILINFOSUM that comes under the title of "comment" is not fact. It is speculation and is speculation issued by the officer or the non-commissioned officer who reads that report and, therefore, only the facts are -- anything under the title of "comment" I would look at and either agree with or disregard. It is not fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you disagree with any of the comment sections that I read from Exhibits 136, 139 or 140?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot agree or disagree with them because they are taken out of a snapshot and you're asking me to turn my mind back to a situation. I can agree that there were a number of points at which the BiH forces wished to cut the road. Those were clearly where the necks and the narrow strips were and it would be to their advantage to do so, but that is a statement almost to the obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that during your tour, the HVO lost more than one-half of the territory of the Vitez/Busovaca enclave to the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be precise, I wouldn't know if it was a half but, yes, they did lose considerable territory to the BiH armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that in addition to defence, Colonel Blaskic's goal during your tour was survival for himself and other Croats in the Vitez/Busovaca pocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree to that and he actually did an extremely successful job in defending the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree he was under extreme pressures in that job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of any formation is under extreme pressure. Somebody said I was under extreme pressure at one stage. It comes and goes. It is something that commanders learn to live with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the MILINFOSUM extract dated 8 August, 1993. Can you help us with the exhibit number, is it 137?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's D-137, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me read this to you. It is short and I have a follow-up question or two. Paragraph 7: "Further details have emerged on the Vitezovi special forces unit operating in the Vitez area. This force was described, along with a number of other units" -- and there's a reference -- "in the distribution list of an HVO CF order as an 'independent unit under the command of the HVO third operational zone commander.' According to Borislav Jozic, a staff officer at operational zone Central Bosnia headquarters, the 'Knights' are an extremist organisation operating throughout Bosnia. The organisation originates from Mostar being commanded by Bruno Stojic. In the Vitez area, the Knights are some 20 to 30 strong and commander Darko Kraljevic, who is a local man from Rijeka. Jozic claimed that the Vitezovi had been responsible for many of the atrocities committed against Muss" -- presumably Muslims. "He further claimed that they were not effectively under Blaskic's control but denied when asked that they worked to Dario Kordic's direction." Do you have any information you can add to this report produced by your unit during your tour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would add that this sort of report was produced from time to time and it is based, as you can see, on the opinions of people who met, whatever rank they were and whatever position they commanded. As I've already stated, I think, sir, the defence of the Vitez pocket relied on forces in territorial positions along with manoeuvre forces and those manoeuvre forces would have to be effective to be under the direct command of the tactical commander and the tactical commander was Colonel Blaskic at that time. They would have to be under his control because he conducted a successful defence, and the reason why that was so successful is he was able to move forces, as I've described before, at speed. To do that, they had to be under his command. He could not afford to leave those forces with anyone else; otherwise, if a problem occurred, he couldn't get hold of them. So you have to keep, as a commander, your manoeuvre forces under your direct control. That's my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to the last extract dated 10th August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is D138.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me read the first, what appears to be part of the paragraph, preceding paragraph, 9: "The Jokeri, (i.e. Jokers) and the 'Vitezovi', (i.e. Knights) are not one and the same unit but are different organisations. The 'Jokeri' are a sub-unit within the 4th BN" -- "Battalion"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that would be normal for "Battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "... 4th Battalion of the HVO Military Police, ("Vojna Policija") with a strength of between 20 and 30 in the Vitez area. They were based in the village of Nadioci" (grid reference). "They are held, by the BiH, to have been held responsible for the massacre at Ahmici" (grid reference). The 'Vitezovi' are independent from the HVO Military Police and operate out of the school in Vitez. The BiH hold them responsible for an alleged massacre in Gacice," (grid reference). "While the 'Jokeri' no longer operate in the Vitez area, the 'Vitezovi' do and continue, according to Borislav Jozic, Operational Zone Central Bosnia," Exchange Officer, "EXCH Officer, to murder BiH prisoners. The leader of the 'Vitezovi' in Vitez, Darko Kraljevic, is a personal friend of Mario Cerkes, Commander of the 'Viteska' HVO Brigade." Brigadier, did you ever hear the allegations made by BiH army officials to you that either the jokers were responsible for massacres in Ahmici or the Vitezovi were responsible for an alleged massacre in Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have heard during my time there allegations of actions by all units against others. I mean, this was not unusual. I wouldn't select this as an unusual event. Accusations were made every day, but they were accusations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic tell you on one or more occasions that any snipers that caused UNPROFOR problems should be shot, that is, UNPROFOR should feel free to shoot to kill those snipers, HVO snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did. We had a -- to explain the background, we had a problem in the camp of snipers firing across our camp, both from the Muslim and the Croat sides, shooting at each other, and I complained about this, and Colonel Blaskic's reply on a number of occasions was, I should shoot those snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you about your meeting with Mr. Valenta. Was Colonel Blaskic present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was Valenta's position; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he have a position in some organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, yes. It was my understanding that Valenta was the HDZ representative for the Vitez area and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The mayor or the head of the party or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the mayor, the representative of that area, and because he was in Vitez with the op zone commander, my assumption was, but I have no proof for it, that he would have had a similar influence over the areas that we've described before as belonging to the op zone commander. A parallel: the military and the political.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Valenta tell you that his book had been adopted by the HDZ as party policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know when the book was published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1991, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So before the war came to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic ever tout to you the contents of Valenta's books as things of value, as ideas having merit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic and I, as far as I remember, avoided talking about political matters because we were military men, and I said often we should just talk about military matters; the politics should be left to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In fact, is it fair to say that Colonel Blaskic never, in any conversation with you, spoke of Muslims with racial prejudice in his statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was -- that's correct, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to the unfortunate subject of your interpreter who was killed. The house in which she was living you have described, and indeed it's depicted in Exhibit 384, was on or near the front-line between the HVO and the BiH army; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, just behind the front-line within the perimeter of the British battalion camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was any available evidence that could constitute the grounds for an investigation other than the fact she was shot by a sniper in her home or outside of her home in the garden? In other words, were there witnesses to the shooting? Were there shell casings recovered at some location that might have been the location that fired upon her or any other evidence of that type, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since those buildings had been occupied for some time by Croats, there would have been shell casings all over the floor anyway, and people had been firing from there. So a technical investigation would have been fairly pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You told us that there was an HVO investigation that blamed a Muslim infiltrator. Was there a report that reached that conclusion; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see a report, no. I was given a verbal brief on the result of the investigation which were that a Muslim had come across from the BiH side, had infiltrated, and had fired from buildings which had been occupied by Croats for some two months, and then had presumably worked his way back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After the murder, did Colonel Blaskic come to see you and offer his personal apology and condolences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you think those were sincerely offered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the UNHCR driver, Boris. Do you know where he was killed in Stari Vitez? Was it on the perimeter or in the middle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was on the perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the perimeter of Stari Vitez a front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that UNPROFOR did a forensic analysis of the car to try and determine the direction from which the projectile came. Were those results shared with the HVO or with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so. They would have been discussed between the LOs, but it was quite clear to us that the bullet came from outside the Stari Vitez pocket. It was not fired from within.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Directing your attention to Exhibit 385, and you may have it in mind -- it can be provided to you also -- this indicates, as I understand it, the general direction of the projectile as reconstructed by your forensic investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very conceptual piece of paper. It is clearly pointing out the rough areas involved. Clearly, with the scale of map involved and the detail being black and white, it merely gives an indication, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether any other evidence existed concerning the murderer who fired this bullet other than this knowledge which your unit gained concerning the direction of fire, such as an eyewitness or forensic analysis of shell casings or forensic analysis of the bullet end, a shell casing, or anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The forensic analysis of the bullet and shell casing would have been pointless because both BiH and HVO were using the same weapons from the same store, so there is little to be gained of that. It is merely the direction of fire that could be established from the strike marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have a few more minutes, but we're nearing the conclusion, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Regarding your sightings of HV troops, in Prozor in 1993, how many HV troops, how many soldiers did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a lorry, a truck, a military truck, and one artillery piece, I think it was 152 millimetre D-30 towed howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many soldiers -- did you see any soldiers with HV patches, or you saw HV licence plates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HV licence plates on the vehicle and two soldiers with HV patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell where they were going to or coming from, or they were static?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were static at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During your tour, did you ever see any HV soldiers in the Lasva or Kiseljak valleys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, do you fault Colonel Blaskic on the subject of prisoners because you believe he did not issue appropriate orders for the release of prisoners? Do you fault him on that basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fault him on the basis that the agreements made at the Joint Military Meetings which we looked at this morning, those pieces of paper in evidence, asked if the orders could be given out, and I think the instructions agreed were quite clear, and I would fault him in not following up on those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what orders for the release of civilian detainees the Prosecutor's Office showed you before or in preparation for your testimony? Did they show you any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen any, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you would be surprised to learn that orders concerning the protection and release of prisoners were issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 18th of April, 1993, the 21st of April, 1993, the 24th of April, 1993, and the 29th of April, 1993, to name a few? That would come as a surprise to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's turn to the subject of trench digging. Would you agree that it was widely known --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hayman. Do you have these elements? Do you have them yourself? Does the Prosecutor have them? Are they in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are Exhibits D32, D39, D77, and D79. They're all in the record of this case. We can take the time and show them to the witness, but, quite frankly, for my purposes it's sufficient that he was asked to give opinion testimony on whether the accused acted properly, and yet he was not shown the orders that the accused in part issued on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if we're going to editorialise on this, the significance is that these are part of the joint command instructions that are given in June that this witness was supposed to undertake, because obviously this was still going on, and no orders subsequent to the first joint command meeting was produced by the Defendant where he reiterated that his soldiers should continue to abide by international humanitarian law. When this particular witness was in theatre pursuant to these particular meetings, Blaskic did nothing, and it just went on. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. That's your opinion there, Mr. Kehoe. I'd like to go back to what the Defence said. These are documents -- do you have these, registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I've got them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could they be shown to the witness so he can tell us whether he recognises them? Excuse me for a moment, Mr. Hayman. I'd like to go to the end of my question. The Judges just allow documents to go back and forth here. I'd like to see what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To assist the registrar, D32, D39, D77, and D79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you would take a look at them, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And they deal with various prisoner-related subjects, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, we don't have them right in front of us, but we know that they're in the file. What is your opinion about these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, if I may, they were all issued by Commander Blaskic before I arrived to take over command of the battalion in Vitez. I have not seen them before. But as far as I'm concerned, clearly, because of the arrangements I had to insist on in June, later on in the year, things had not happened. So despite these orders being issued, we still had to go through a system and insist they were reissued later on. But my comment on these: It was before the time I took over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. You mean there was no follow-up of these orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, by whom, sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: By General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that at all, I'm afraid. The orders were issued before I arrived. I think that the last one, about five or six days before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. This has been clarified. I think that they can be put back into the file. Mr. Hayman, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Brigadier, would you agree that it was known within the Vitez-Busovaca enclave that the BiH army was using Croat prisoners to dig trenches, that that was generally known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was generally known.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In your movements in the theatre, did you ever personally see HVO soldiers with forced labour, that is, Muslim prisoners being compelled to dig trenches? Is that something you personally saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never personally saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have mentioned the subject of helicopters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I have to say, by the way you phrased that and the fact that we moved through it and passed it, you imply that because the BiH Army was using Croats to dig trenches, it was perfectly all right for the Croats to use BiH to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please, Brigadier, I don't imply anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You're jumping to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the inference I took. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's not an inference I'm suggesting to the Court in the least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Then the question is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No. I'll state the relevance of the question, Mr. President, if you want to take the time to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If the question is asked about whether or not it is well-known that the BiH was forcing Croats to dig trenches, what could that question bear on except to insinuate to the Brigadier, in much the same way that he took that insinuation, is that because the Croats -- because the Muslims were doing it, it was okay for the Croats to do it, the old tu quoque argument which, of course, is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's not okay for anyone to do it, Mr. President. The point is, if you have a population in the Vitez pocket and a population in Zenica and they believe that their counterparts are taking civilians hostage to use an exchange, are using civilians to dig trenches, it makes it all the more difficult for the authorities, military, civilian, to control the situation and control those civilians that have that knowledge and those beliefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're saying. But you are falling right into the objection of the witness, that there is an idea behind your question. Everybody has understood what was said. The witness has answered. Let's move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Helicopters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There were Medevac evacuations from Novi Bila. Were U.N. helicopters moved to Medevac out of Novi Bila from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The system we had for Novi Bila, which was, I believe, a Franciscan -- or a church outside -- in the pocket, rather, was that we would use helicopters from Kiseljak and we would transport the wounded where we could in ambulances from Vitez to Kiseljak along the main road escorted by United Nations vehicles and they would be flown out from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: By U.N. helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe we also used Croatian helicopters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that you believed that one or more times during your tour, Colonel Blaskic left the Vitez enclave for a period of days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the first time that you believe he was able to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't put a precise time on it, but it was apparent, from the fact that I couldn't get hold of Colonel Blaskic when I wanted to, that he wasn't there, and -- I mean, it clearly wasn't in his interests to let people know he was gone because, you know, if people know generally that a commander is away, it's an opportunity to take some action while he's gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us that the first time you believed he was absent was in the fall of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would have been -- looking at the way events occurred there, I think Colonel Blaskic would obviously have been extremely busy during the time that the BiH were advancing. Once the situation had stabilised and we had pockets and he had a good defence, he then felt that the -- you know, things were holding out well and perhaps he had an opportunity to get out then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And when would that have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would have been about the fall, by the autumn-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that any helicopter coming into the Vitez pocket without an agreement for safe passage by the BiH army would be in some jeopardy of being fired upon and hit by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my experience that all helicopters, regardless of where they belong to, are always in jeopardy when they fly in a war zone because nobody takes much notice of whether it's friendly. The helicopters arrived without agreement from BiH and they arrived with agreement from BiH. In general terms, agreement was either too late or unspecific, but the helicopters flew at fairly regular intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they generally fly at night because of the danger of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They flew at night and with a very skilful pilot who was able to fly in a spiral down at high speed from an altitude in order to avoid getting hit by anti-aircraft fires or missiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that a dangerous manoeuvre, potentially dangerous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's an extremely dangerous manoeuvre requiring a very skilled pilot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have the pleasure of being on one of these helicopters that spiralled down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that would -- I didn't go in HVO helicopters, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fortunately. Fortunately, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have just a few more questions, Mr. President and Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that Colonel Blaskic was accepted and was accepted politically as demonstrated by his subsequent promotion. Did you have occasion to meet Philip Filipovic, an HVO officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, there were a number of Filipovics. Are we referring an officer who was the second in command of the op zone?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Philip Filipovic, at one time the brigade commander in Travnik; and then after Travnik fell, he located obviously somewhere else in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe, and I might be wrong, but I believe he moved into the headquarters in Vitez. He was quite badly affected by events in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he feel that he had been double-crossed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just think he felt -- I mean, he had been defeated. I don't think there's a question of double-crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was he accepted and politically acceptable to the HVO, do you know, Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was he subsequently promoted to General within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have previously said that the defence of the Vitez pocket was dependent on the HVO control of the spinal road from Novi Travnik to Vitez to Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, just to illustrate that principle, about Grbavica. There was a Muslim village at Grbavica; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is immediately adjacent to the BRITBAT base and to the north of this spinal road or MSR, Main Supply Route; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And there was, in the fall of 1993, a military action to take control of that village; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it your view that that action was a bona fide military action in order to secure the MSR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military action or the aim of the military action to secure the high ground to the north of that major -- or Main Supply Route was a legitimate business. It did take place in the autumn. It took place the day after I left for two weeks' leave, and I have mentioned before taking advantage of commanders being away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would that military action also require control of the village on the top of the hill because the local population was armed and itself constituted a defensive military force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a requirement to get to the buildings on top of the hill because they represented a good defensive area, which is why it had held out for so long. There was not a requirement, in my opinion, to destroy those buildings, which is what happened, because the military worth of the buildings were -- on the top of the hill was they provided the cover and protection and ability to hold a strong defensive position, which is what they've done. By setting fire to them, which is what happened after the initial assault, that achieved no -- to my mind, to my personal opinion, no military purpose whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, by contrast to the defence of the enclave, which you've described, did you conclude that the roads and towns inside the Vitez pocket were an internal security matter more under the control of local politicians than under the control of Colonel Blaskic? And I'm citing, quoting from page 4 of your prior statement, if you'd like to review it, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, that -- that may well have been an opinion at that time, and I'm well aware this statement was made in, I think, April of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me read it to you so we can be absolutely clear what your opinion was: "The control of the military operations troops was made directly by Colonel Blaskic and the internal security was controlled by Dario Kordic in conjunction with Blaskic. It appeared to me that Blaskic was responsible for military defence, but roads, towns, et cetera, inside the pocket were internal security, hence more under the control of local politicians and therefore Kordic." Was that your statement of 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you also say in your statement, page 14: "I believe that the political organisation was responsible for the forced ethnic movement in this area." "This area" referring to the Lasva Valley; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's who generated the responsibility, but obviously that has to be then done by -- it has to be done by military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you also say, and I believe it's at the same passage, that Tihomir Blaskic -- you do not believe that Blaskic was close to these individuals, referring to the individuals in the political organisation in the Lasva Valley. That's the top of the next paragraph. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I stated in this. But as I've stated before, in the light of my preparations and for the first time since I left Bosnia, having a look at the events that took place then -- and I made that statement last year -- you know, that was made at that time. For a number of reasons, after I had left Bosnia, I was not particularly interested in analysing in great detail what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How much time have you spent analysing these questions in the last year since your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since my statement? Some time since I made the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not at the request, it was when I received it back through the post, having taken a transcript, I looked at it in detail then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that before or after you signed it, that you looked it over in detail? Was that before or after you signed the statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I signed it, because it was a true record of the meeting and what I had spoken about at the time. I mean, the point I'm trying to make is I may have been very wrong in some of my assumptions which were based on my personal opinions. That is all, sir. That's the point I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You told me last summer when we spoke that you believed Tihomir Blaskic was "a reasonable and honest man trying to do a job in the most difficult circumstances." Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Have you -- I was never supplied with a copy of your transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you told that you could see it, if you wanted to, by the British military authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I understood you were going to send me a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, that -- again, I shouldn't be answering questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why don't we -- do you agree with the statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with that. I said that at the time, yes, in the knowledge at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. I think we'll take a break about ten after four, if we can finish by then, unless there are many questions. Mr. Kehoe, do you have a lot of questions you wish to ask? Of course, you're free to ask any questions you want. Put on the microphone, please. I'm sure you're making a joke, but, I'm sorry, the joke might have got lost now because the microphone was off. Let me consult with my colleague for a moment. I think minds need calm. Perhaps the General needs a little bit of rest as well. So I think we'll start again in about 20 minutes. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now. Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I neglected to offer Exhibits D-135 through D-140.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. They have been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, I would like to ask you some questions based on counsel's questions during cross, if I may. So to the extent that I jump around a bit from topic to topic, bear with me. You were asked some questions about the first report of the 19th of June, 1993 about the meeting of the first joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked some questions by Defence counsel that this was a time, a very difficult time, for the defendant Blaskic in that Travnik had just fallen, many displaced people are coming in. This was a period of time, was it not, when Blaskic thought that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say also that during this time, Blaskic was trying to have you help him and trying to have you assist him should such an attack come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, at this stage, it was clearly in his interest since he was on the back foot, as it were, to have as much assistance as he could from U.N.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that at this point it would not be in his interest to alienate you at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't. It would not be a sensible thing to do, to annoy me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to Prosecutor's Exhibit 386 which is that first meeting of the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Claudius, with your assistance --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I interject? I just note for the court that the court admonished me not to examine this witness on these four reports if I wished to preserve my objection under Rule 66(a), and I did not cross-examine the witness about any one of those four reports based on the court's admonition because we do wish to preserve that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President and Judge Riad, I think we had some very significant questions by Defence counsel, my colleague across the room, concerning these orders, these unnumbered orders from April of 1993 that he argued that we didn't show to the brigadier. In order to follow up the inferences that one might draw from counsel's questions, we need to draw ourselves back to Exhibit 386 and then we will go back to the particular exhibits that counsel asked the brigadier about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm a bit uncomfortable, Mr. Kehoe. At the end of the morning, I did say to Mr. Nobilo and to Mr. Hayman that in the judges' minds the documents had already been tendered, that they would be tendered. I said that if they are tendered, it would be this afternoon and Defence counsel could then use them. I believe from that point on he would give up his objection. I would say that the Defence has not asked any questions. You should ask questions only as part of the cross-examination or in scope of the cross-examination. I prefer that you don't use them right now because they still must be admitted by the judges. It's true we have kept this possibility for ourselves. Therefore, I would prefer that you not use that document because it was not used or quoted or referred to in the course of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge. I can proceed with the documents that counsel was waving about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that you could ask your question without referring to that document, so we won't use them right now. Ask the questions but please remain within the scope of the cross-examination. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you received, I think that you said that your fax machine -- well, maybe you didn't say this, but your fax machine was rather active with faxes coming from the defendant, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be, yes. That was a primary means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He clogged your machine up from time to time with correspondence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he ever show you these orders that Defence counsel just gave you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he ever say anything about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not a word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In every meeting that you had with him between May and November of 1993, he never said a word about these unnumbered documents that Defence counsel has just discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. Now, counsel asked you some questions about the radio communications in the area. I think he asked you some questions about power in the area --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- difficulties with power in the area, and you mentioned something that armies generally have a backup generator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generators, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Blaskic ever indicate to you that he did not know what was going on in the areas under his control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He never said, "I don't know what's going on over there." It was the reverse. I mean, he was telling me what was going on in the other areas under his control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm jumping to another topic which has to do with Kiseljak, and we talked on direct and you were asked some questions by counsel about Kiseljak and the geographical separation between the Vitez pocket and the Vitez pocket (sic). Then you were asked some questions, I recall, by Defence on cross-examination, and this didn't come up on direct, this was cross-examination questions, that in Rakovica on the 10th of June of 1993, on the first day that the Convoy of Joy was coming through, General Petkovic and his military police entourage was going down the road and you stopped them and spoke to them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you spoke to them to try to gain their assistance to get through that checkpoint; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was to get through the block on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your direct examination, you testified that on the 29th of May, 1993, you met with Petkovic, the defendant and some other HVO leaders in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then some 11 days later, Petkovic, he was a General, was he not? He's probably at least the chief of staff or maybe general of the army at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He is in the Vitez area on the 10th; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How did he get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't bring him in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did BRITBAT bring him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we had a policy of not ferrying people around. As a result of the meeting in Kiseljak on the 29th, a policy was established that we certainly wouldn't move people around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Outside U.N. and outside any taxi service in the U.N., the General of the HVO somehow made it from Kiseljak to Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And he was driving back out towards the Novi Travnik road; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was off down towards Prozor, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he in an armoured personnel carrier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was in a 4-by-4 Shogun or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Brigadier, that in the General of the HVO, General Petkovic, an important guy, I would think, if General Petkovic could make that trip between Kiseljak and Vitez in something other than an armoured personnel carrier, the defendant could too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the inference must be that -- yeah, I mean, I don't see why not. If General Petkovic can drive around, then others could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it indicate to you that they were doing it? Did it indicate to you that they thought it was safe enough to make that trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think Petkovic would have embarked on the trip if he didn't think it was a safe way to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let's talk a little bit about the Convoy of Joy issue. You were asked some questions about Petkovic's conduct when you were trying to elicit his help. These are questions on cross. You noted that the -- why don't you tell us: When you asked Petkovic for his help, what did he do? How did he act to you? What was his body language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He just laughed at me and that was it and then just disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he speak to the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He spoke to the -- as I said, he spoke to the crowd there, and they appeared to be pleased with what he had said. And then laughing and smiling, I asked him with my interpreter whether we could go through and he said, no and laughed and just drove off through the crowd which parted to let him go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he ever order his soldiers to go in there and separate these civilians off the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked some questions on cross-examination as to whether or not those soldiers who were beating that, I'm assuming, a Muslim truck driver and who were looting those pieces of property, whether or not they were off duty or on duty. Now, Brigadier, you have been in the British Army 25 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You have, I assume, as a commander of Prince of Wales of Yorkshire and also in your other capacities as an officer, discipline your troops. Did you ever discipline your troops for conduct that happened off duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no difference in the British Army between either off or on duty. You're a soldier 24 hours a day, peace time as well as in operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted in response to a question in direct and also on cross -- let me withdraw that question. Would you say that with regard to the conduct of those soldiers, a commanding officer's duty to discipline stays in effect whether or not those soldiers are off duty or on duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very much so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was the conduct or what happened with the Convoy of Joy on the 10th of June and the 11th of June, 1993 and the looting and the shooting and the killing a well-known fact in that area at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, that it had happened -- I'm not quite sure what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me ask you very frankly, Brigadier. Is it likely that Blaskic wouldn't have known about the deaths of these truck drivers and about the looting by his soldiers and about the rest of the relevance attendant to the attack on the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's very unlikely that he didn't know because everybody was out. There were clearly arrangements. There were people everywhere being organised to block things. Trucks were being cut out. The trucks were not just limited to a certain area. They ended up all over the town of Vitez in little packets being looted. They were separated out in a coordinated plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was any attempt made by Blaskic to discipline those troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is a commander who told you on numerous times about his inability to control extremists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall a message going over Radio Vitez in August of 1993 concerning the relations between the UNPROFOR and the HVO and what Radio Kiseljak reported that the HVO commanders said concerning their troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The message was that there could be no guarantee of the safety of UNPROFOR troops and white vehicles in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did they not also say that the HVO commanding officers were no longer responsible for the actions of their troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that was the text, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was the head commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was Commander Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On Radio Vitez, in his area where his headquarters are, an announcement comes over that a commanding officer could no longer control his troops; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. That's what the announcement was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In that same message, was there any threat passed over to white vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They mentioned white vehicles. They could no longer guarantee -- this included white vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are way past the scope of direct, nor is there any foundation concerning the accused's control over Radio Kiseljak or Radio Vitez. In fact, there's been testimony to the contrary, and I think there's an ethical question about the testimony being elicited on the part of Prosecution counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I understand that it's very harmful to the Defence; however, the HVO --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's not harmful at all, Mr. President, but there's an ethical question where testimony has been elicited that Radio Kiseljak, for example, was under the control of political elements in the Kiseljak enclave, and that raises an ethical question for Mr. Kehoe concerning the testimony he is attempting to elicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand that Defence counsel doesn't like what the testimony is to be elicited, Judge Riad and Judge Jorda, but the HVO commanding officers were Blaskic and his commanding officers who put an announcement over the radio in Vitez that they could no longer control their troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. The message has gone through. General, did this message go through the radio, the message from the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think you can ask the question. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
